blocks.content: The http-basics topic established that HTTP is stateless by default, each request treated completely independently, with no built in memory connecting it to any other. Cookies are the actual mechanism invented specifically to fix this, letting a website recognize the same browser across many separate requests despite that fundamental statelessness.

If you have ever stayed logged into a website across multiple page visits, or had a shopping cart remember its contents as you kept browsing, cookies were almost certainly doing that work invisibly underneath.

When a server wants to remember something about a particular browser, it includes a Set-Cookie header in its response. The browser receiving this response stores that cookie locally, associated with that specific website.

Once stored, the browser automatically attaches that same cookie to every future request it sends to that same website, with no extra effort required from the user, or even from the specific page being loaded. This automatic attachment is exactly what gives the server its working memory across otherwise independent requests.

Putting both directions together completes the picture. The very first request to a site has no cookie yet. The server response sets one. The browser stores it. Every later request to that same site automatically includes that same cookie, letting the server recognize this is the same browser it has seen before.

At its core, a cookie is a simple name and value pair, a small piece of data the server chose to store. Alongside that core data, a cookie also carries several attributes, including an expiration, which specific domain it belongs to, and security related flags covered later in this topic.

blocks.title: Cookies are genuinely small
blocks.content: A single cookie is typically limited to just a few kilobytes, and browsers cap how many a single site can set. Cookies are meant for small identifiers and preferences, not for storing large amounts of actual data.

Staying logged into a website across separate page visits, a shopping cart remembering its contents as you keep browsing, a site remembering a preference you set, like a chosen language or theme, are all genuinely everyday, common uses of exactly this mechanism.

An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by page scripts at all, only by the browser itself when actually sending requests, protecting against certain kinds of script based attacks trying to steal it. A Secure cookie is only ever sent over an actual HTTPS connection, covered in the sibling https topic, never over a plain, unencrypted one, protecting it from being exposed in transit.

blocks.title: Why these flags genuinely matter
blocks.content: A cookie often holds something sensitive, like proof you are logged in. Without these protections, that sensitive value could potentially be stolen by malicious scripts or exposed on an unencrypted connection, either one a real, practical security risk.

A session cookie has no expiration set at all, and simply disappears the moment the browser closes. A persistent cookie has a real expiration date set, and survives across browser restarts, continuing to work until it genuinely expires or is deliberately deleted.

items: Assuming a cookie is automatically sent to every website, when it is only ever sent back to the specific domain it was originally set for.
Storing something genuinely sensitive in a cookie without the HttpOnly and Secure flags, leaving it needlessly exposed to real, practical attacks.
Cookies exist specifically to give stateless HTTP a working memory across separate requests.
A server sets a cookie, and the browser automatically attaches it to every later request to that same site.
HttpOnly and Secure are genuinely important protections, not optional extras, for anything sensitive.
A session cookie disappears when the browser closes; a persistent cookie survives until its expiration.
